entries.content:
> Source : GitHub sorrycc/awesome-javascript — README.md — licence voir le dépôt

## Reactive Programming
*Reactive programming libraries to extend JavaScript’s capabilities.*

* [RxJS](https://github.com/ReactiveX/rxjs) - A reactive programming library for JavaScript.
* [Bacon](https://github.com/baconjs/bacon.js) - FRP (functional reactive programming) library for JavaScript.
* [Kefir](https://github.com/pozadi/kefir) - FRP library for JavaScript inspired by Bacon.js and RxJS with focus on high performance and low memory consumption.
* [Highland](https://caolan.github.io/highland/) - Re-thinking the JavaScript utility belt, Highland manages synchronous and asynchronous code easily, using nothing more than standard JavaScript and Node-like Streams.
* [Most.js](https://github.com/cujojs/most) - high performance FRP library.
* [MobX](https://github.com/mobxjs/mobx) - TFRP library for simple, scalable state management.
* [Cycle.js](https://cycle.js.org) - A functional and reactive JavaScript library for cleaner code.
* [concent](https://github.com/concentjs/concent) - Definitely the ❤️ simplest but ⚡️ strongest state management for react, it is predictable、progressive and efficient.
* [stunk](https://github.com/I-am-abdulazeez/stunk) A framework-agnostic state management library that keeps your app’s state clean and simple. It uses a fine-grained state model, breaking state into independent, manageable chunks.

## Data Structure
*Data structure libraries to build a more sophisticated application.*

* [immutable-js](https://github.com/facebook/immutable-js) - Immutable Data Collections including Sequence, Range, Repeat, Map, OrderedMap, Set and a sparse Vector.
* [mori](https://github.com/swannodette/mori) - A library for using ClojureScript's persistent data structures and supporting API from the comfort of vanilla JavaScript.
* [buckets](https://github.com/mauriciosantos/Buckets-JS) - A complete, fully tested and documented data structure library written in JavaScript.
* [hashmap](https://github.com/flesler/hashmap) - Simple hashmap implementation that supports any kind of keys.
* [ngraph.graph](https://github.com/anvaka/ngraph.graph) - Graph data structure in javascript.
* [js-sdsl](https://github.com/zly201/js-sdsl) - Refer to the javascript standard data structure library implemented by c++ stl, which supports c++ bidirectional iterator mode.

## Date
*Date Libraries.*

* [moment](https://github.com/moment/moment) - Parse, validate, manipulate, and display dates in JavaScript.
* [moment-timezone](https://github.com/moment/moment-timezone) - Timezone support for moment.js.
* [jquery-timeago](https://github.com/rmm5t/jquery-timeago) - A jQuery plugin that makes it easy to support automatically updating fuzzy timestamps (e.g. "4 minutes ago").
* [timezone-js](https://github.com/mde/timezone-js) - Timezone-enabled JavaScript Date object. Uses Olson zoneinfo files for timezone data.
* [date](https://github.com/MatthewMueller/date) - Date() for humans.
* [ms.js](https://github.com/rauchg/ms.js) - Tiny millisecond conversion utility.
* [countdown.js](https://github.com/gumroad/countdown.js) - Super simple countdowns.
* [timeago.js](https://github.com/hustcc/timeago.js) - Simple library (less then 2kb) used to format date with `*** time ago` statement.
* [fecha](https://github.com/taylorhakes/fecha) - Lightweight date formatting and parsing (~2KB). Meant to replace parsing and formatting functionality of moment.js.
* [date-fns](https://github.com/date-fns/date-fns) - Modern JavaScript date utility library.
* [map-countdown](https://github.com/dawidjaniga/map-countdown) - A browser countdown built on top of the Google Maps.
* [dayjs](https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs) - Day.js 2KB immutable date library alternative to Moment.js with the same modern API.
* [luxon](https://github.com/moment/luxon) - Luxon is a library for working with dates and times in JavaScript.
* [tempo](https://github.com/formkit/tempo) - Parsing, formatting, and timezones — Tempo is a small tree-shakable library for native Date objects.

## String
*String Libraries.*

* [voca](https://github.com/panzerdp/voca) - The ultimate JavaScript string library
* [selecting](https://github.com/EvandroLG/selecting) - A library that allows you to access the text selected by the user.
* [underscore.string](https://github.com/epeli/underscore.string) - String manipulation extensions for Underscore.js JavaScript library.
* [string.js](https://github.com/jprichardson/string.js) - Extra JavaScript string methods.
* [he](https://github.com/mathiasbynens/he) - A robust HTML entity encoder/decoder written in JavaScript.
* [multiline](https://github.com/sindresorhus/multiline) - Multiline strings in JavaScript.
* [query-string](https://github.com/sindresorhus/query-string) - Parse and stringify URL query strings.
* [URI.js](https://github.com/medialize/URI.js/) - JavaScript URL mutation library.
* [jsurl](https://github.com/Mikhus/domurl) - Lightweight URL manipulation with JavaScript.
* [sprintf.js](https://github.com/alexei/sprintf.js) - A sprintf implementation.
* [url-pattern](https://github.com/snd/url-pattern) - Easier than regex string matching patterns for urls and other strings. Turn strings into data or data into strings.
* [plexis](https://github.com/plexis-js/plexis) - Lo-fi, powerful, community-driven string manipulation library.
* [url-state-machine](https://github.com/anonrig/url-js) - Super fast spec-compliant URL parser state machine for Node.js.

## Number

* [Numeral-js](https://github.com/adamwdraper/Numeral-js) - A JavaScript library for formatting and manipulating numbers.
* [chance.js](https://github.com/chancejs/chancejs) - Random generator helper in JavaScript. Can generate numbers, strings etc.
* [odometer](https://github.com/HubSpot/odometer) - Smoothly transitions numbers with ease.
* [accounting.js](https://github.com/josscrowcroft/accounting.js) - A lightweight JavaScript library for number, money and currency formatting - fully localisable, zero dependencies.
* [money.js](https://github.com/josscrowcroft/money.js) - A tiny (1kb) JavaScript currency conversion library, for web & nodeJS.

3. **Mobile Performance Optimization**: You will ensure smooth performance by:
   - Implementing efficient list virtualization
   - Optimizing image loading and caching
   - Minimizing bridge calls in React Native
   - Using native animations when possible
   - Profiling and fixing memory leaks
   - Reducing app startup time

4. **Platform Integration**: You will leverage native features by:
   - Implementing push notifications (FCM/APNs)
   - Adding biometric authentication
   - Integrating with device cameras and sensors
   - Handling deep linking and app shortcuts
   - Implementing in-app purchases
   - Managing app permissions properly

5. **Mobile UI/UX Implementation**: You will create native experiences by:
   - Following iOS Human Interface Guidelines
   - Implementing Material Design on Android
   - Creating smooth page transitions
   - Handling keyboard interactions properly
   - Implementing pull-to-refresh patterns
   - Supporting dark mode across platforms

6. **App Store Optimization**: You will prepare for launch by:
   - Optimizing app size and startup time
   - Implementing crash reporting and analytics
   - Creating App Store/Play Store assets
   - Handling app updates gracefully
   - Implementing proper versioning
   - Managing beta testing through TestFlight/Play Console

**Technology Expertise**:
- iOS: Swift, SwiftUI, UIKit, Combine
- Android: Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Coroutines
- Cross-Platform: React Native, Flutter, Expo
- Backend: Firebase, Amplify, Supabase
- Testing: XCTest, Espresso, Detox

**Mobile-Specific Patterns**:
- Offline-first architecture
- Optimistic UI updates
- Background task handling
- State preservation
- Deep linking strategies
- Push notification patterns

**Performance Targets**:
- App launch time < 2 seconds
- Frame rate: consistent 60fps
- Memory usage < 150MB baseline
- Battery impact: minimal
- Network efficiency: bundled requests
- Crash rate < 0.1%

**Platform Guidelines**:
- iOS: Navigation patterns, gestures, haptics
- Android: Back button handling, material motion
- Tablets: Responsive layouts, split views
- Accessibility: VoiceOver, TalkBack support
- Localization: RTL support, dynamic sizing

Your goal is to create mobile applications that feel native, perform excellently, and delight users with smooth interactions. You understand that mobile users have high expectations and low tolerance for janky experiences. In the rapid development environment, you balance quick deployment with the quality users expect from mobile apps.

entries.title: Prompt : Professional Full-Stack Developer for Network Mapping & Monitoring Application
entries.content:
Modèle de prompt prêt à l'emploi : **Professional Full-Stack Developer for Network Mapping & Monitoring Application**.
À copier dans le chat ou l'Atelier IA d'Ivass, en adaptant les parties entre ${…}.

---

Act as a professional full-stack developer. You are tasked with developing a web application for **Mapping & Monitoring Networks** connected to the Mikrotik Netwatch API.

Your objectives include:
- Building a role-based multi-user system to manage devices and monitor their status (UP/DOWN).
- Mapping devices on an interactive map and managing user balances for device subscriptions.

Step-by-step instructions:

1. **Project Structure Setup**
   - Define tables: users, roles, devices, device_types, ports, connections, logs, routers, and user_balances.
   - Provide a normalized schema design with foreign key relationships.

2. **Authentication & Authorization**
   - Implement a multi-user system with login & session management.
   - Roles: Admin and User.
   - Admin can manage users, roles, and routers.
   - Users can only manage devices according to their balance.

3. **User & Balance Management**
   - CRUD operations for users (Admin only).
   - Each user has a balance.
   - Subscription model: Rp.250 per device/month.
   - Automatically deduct balance monthly based on device addition date.
   - Prevent device addition if balance is insufficient.

4. **Device Type Management (CRUD)**
   - Devices can be "manageable" or "unmanageable".
   - If manageable, assign IP addresses per port.

5. **Device Management (CRUD)**
   - Add devices with port count and name.
   - Assign IP addresses to each port if the device is manageable.
   - Add devices by clicking on a map (coordinates) → pop-up form appears.

6. **Connection Management**
   - Connect devices by selecting source & destination ports.
   - Assign IP addresses to connections.
   - Move connections to other available ports.
   - Remove connections.

7. **Integration with Mikrotik Netwatch API**
   - Monitor devices based on assigned IPs.
   - Retrieve UP/DOWN status.
   - Log device status changes.

8. **Monitoring Dashboard**
   - Display devices on a map with various view styles.
   - Use different icon colors for UP/DOWN status.
   - Show device status change history logs.

9. **Remote Device Access**
   - Add a "Remote" button for each device.
   - Clicking the button automatically creates a port forwarding rule in Mikrotik (src-port specified, dst-port random).
   - Add/remove port forwarding rules.

10. **Multi Router Implementation**
   - Each user can have more than one Mikrotik router as a Netwatch server.
   - Save router assignments per user.

11. **Interactive Map**
   - Visualize all devices and connections.
   - Support various map display styles.

12. **Logging & Audit Trail**
   - Save UP/DOWN history for each device.
   - Save user action history (add/remove device, connection, port forwarding).

13. **Security & Best Practices**
   - Validate all API requests.
   - Protect the application from SQL Injection, XSS, CSRF.
   - Use secure authentication for Mikrotik API.

entries.title: Prompt : The Data Detective
entries.content:
Modèle de prompt prêt à l'emploi : **The Data Detective**.
À copier dans le chat ou l'Atelier IA d'Ivass, en adaptant les parties entre ${…}.

---

You are a healthcare data analyst and project management strategist. I'm going to give you project data, and I need you to be a Data Detective — don't just summarize, INVESTIGATE.

**Data I'm Providing:** [PASTE YOUR DATA — could be project metrics, utilization data, budget reports, quality scores, survey results, timeline tracking, etc.]

Perform this investigation:

**1. First Impressions (The Headlines)**
- What are the 3 most important things this data is screaming at you?
- What's the single most surprising finding?

**2. Pattern Recognition**
- What trends are emerging? (improving, declining, cyclical, flat)
- Are there correlations between variables that suggest cause-and-effect?
- What patterns would a non-analyst miss?

**3. Anomaly Detection**
- What numbers don't make sense or seem off?
- Where are the outliers, and what might explain them?
- What data is suspiciously perfect (possible data quality issue)?

**4. The Missing Data**
- What data SHOULD be here but isn't?
- What questions can't you answer with what's provided?
- What additional data would change the analysis?

**5. So What? (The Actionable Insights)**
- For each key finding, provide: Finding → Implication → Recommended Action
- Prioritize by impact and urgency

**6. The Story**
- Write a 3-sentence narrative summary suitable for an executive audience
- Write a 1-paragraph technical summary for the project team

Be direct. Be specific. Don't hedge — tell me what the data says.

entries.title: Méthode : Organiser le montage
entries.content:
# Méthode : Organiser le montage
**Objectif :** Modifier l'ordre ou supprimer des séquences.
**Source :** Comment Créer des Vidéos IA Gratuites qui Parlent avec Google Veo 3.1 (Tutoriel Flow) — Alpa14 ([16:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QVD8kZi4GTA&t=998s))

1. Cliquer sur 'Organiser'
2. Utiliser le bouton '-' pour supprimer une scène
3. Glisser-déposer les scènes pour changer l'ordre
4. Valider avec 'OK'

**Pièges signalés dans la vidéo :**
- Le plan gratuit de Gemini limite la génération à environ une dizaine d'images par jour.
- Attention au format de l'image (vertical vs 16/9) lors de l'importation dans Flow pour éviter les problèmes de cadrage.
- Le mode 'Quality' consomme 100 crédits d'un coup, ce qui peut vider votre compte gratuit en une seule génération.
- Les transitions automatiques peuvent créer des doublons d'images (les derniers instants d'une scène sont identiques aux premiers de la suivante).
- La voix générée par défaut peut avoir un rendu métallique dû à la compression sonore.

entries.title: Comparatif IA 2026 : ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini ou Copilot ?
entries.content:
Tech
## Comparatif IA 2026 : ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini ou Copilot ?
GPT-6, Claude 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon ou Microsoft Copilot : versions disponibles, fenêtres de contexte et tarifs officiels pour choisir le bon assistant IA.
Stéphane Larue Journaliste — article rédigé avec l’IA Publié le 29 mars 2026 à 19h13 Mis à jour le 16 octobre 2026 à 04h43
7 min de lecture
Image générée par IA Publicité
Au sommaire
- Ce qui a changé depuis septembre : GPT-6, Claude 5.5 et Gemini 4 Argon
- ChatGPT passe à GPT-6 dans toutes ses offres
- Claude lit un million de tokens d’un seul tenant
- Gemini 3.1 Pro s’active dans Gmail, Docs et Sheets
- Microsoft 365 Copilot Business coûte 15,60 € par mois et par utilisateur
- Aucun ne domine partout, c’est le contexte qui tranche
ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini ou Microsoft Copilot : le choix d’un assistant IA se joue moins sur la puissance brute que sur l’endroit où vous travaillez déjà. Versions disponibles, fenêtres de contexte et tarifs officiels, vérifiés chez chaque éditeur.
## Ce qui a changé depuis septembre : GPT-6, Claude 5.5 et Gemini 4 Argon
OpenAI a commencé à déployer GPT-6 dans ChatGPT le 7 octobre 2026, d’abord dans les offres payantes, puis le 8 octobre dans les offres gratuite et Go.
Publicité
Chez Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5 est sorti le 22 septembre 2026 et Claude Sonnet 5.5 le 28 septembre. Claude Haiku 5.5 complète désormais la gamme.
Google a ouvert largement Gemini 4 Argon le 13 octobre 2026. C’est son nouveau modèle de pointe.
À lire aussi
- Intelligence artificielle : ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude et toute l’actualité de l’IA
## ChatGPT passe à GPT-6 dans toutes ses offres
Selon OpenAI, GPT-6 est le modèle par défaut de ChatGPT depuis le 7 octobre 2026 : GPT-6 Sol pour les abonnés Plus, Pro, Business et Enterprise, GPT-6 Luna pour les offres gratuite et Go.
OpenAI avait présenté GPT-5.6 Sol le 26 juin 2026, d’abord proposé par l’API et par Codex à un groupe restreint de partenaires. GPT-6 l’a remplacé comme modèle principal, mais GPT-5.6 Sol reste sélectionnable dans le menu des modèles.
Son atout reste la polyvalence. Rédaction, résumés, traduction, code, analyse de documents : ChatGPT couvre tous ces usages sans configuration particulière.
Pour qui : les indépendants, les équipes créatives, et tous ceux qui ne sont pas enfermés dans un écosystème logiciel.
## Claude lit un million de tokens d’un seul tenant
La documentation d’Anthropic recense quatre modèles actuels : Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 et Claude Haiku 5.5. Opus 5 et Sonnet 5 sont désormais classés parmi les anciens modèles, toujours disponibles.
Les quatre acceptent désormais une fenêtre de contexte d’ un million de tokens et produisent jusqu’à 128 000 tokens en sortie. Haiku 5.5 reste le plus rapide de la gamme.
Concrètement, un million de tokens représente plusieurs centaines de pages. C’est ce qui permet de soumettre un dossier entier, un contrat ou une base de code sans le découper.
Anthropic recommande désormais Opus 5.5 comme point de départ pour la plupart des usages, et Fable 5.1 pour le raisonnement exigeant et les tâches d’agent qui s’étalent dans le temps. Sonnet 5.5 offre, selon l’éditeur, le meilleur compromis entre vitesse et intelligence.
Pour qui : les juristes, les chercheurs, les développeurs, et les rédacteurs qui travaillent sur de longs formats.
## Gemini 3.1 Pro s’active dans Gmail, Docs et Sheets
Google DeepMind propose quatre déclinaisons : Gemini 3.1 Pro , Gemini 3.1 Deep Think, Gemini 3.8 Flash et Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.
Depuis le 13 octobre 2026, Google y ajoute Gemini 4 Argon. Il est accessible aux abonnés Google AI Pro et Ultra dans l’application Gemini, ainsi qu’aux développeurs par l’API, avec une limite d’un million de tokens.
Publicité
Sur les tests publiés par DeepMind, Gemini 3.8 Flash obtient 89,4 % sur Terminal-bench 2.1 et 73,7 % sur DeepSWE v1.1.
Mais l’argument de Google n’est pas là. Gemini fonctionne directement dans Gmail, Google Docs, Google Sheets et Google Meet : pour une équipe déjà sur Workspace, l’assistant s’active sans changer d’onglet.
Pour qui : les équipes Google Workspace et les analystes qui travaillent sur Google Cloud.
## Microsoft 365 Copilot Business coûte 15,60 € par mois et par utilisateur
Copilot ne cherche pas à être le plus performant en dehors de Microsoft 365, mais le plus intégré à l’intérieur : Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook et Teams.
Votre argent, vos droits Versement retraite novembre 2026 : Agirc-Arrco le lundi 2, Cnav le lundi 9 novembre → La page de tarifs française de Microsoft affiche le complément Copilot Business à 15,60 € HT par utilisateur et par mois en paiement annuel, contre 21,84 € HT en paiement mensuel.
Les formules groupées reviennent à 20,36 € HT par mois avec Microsoft 365 Business Standard, et à 27,73 € HT avec Business Premium, toujours en engagement annuel. Un mois d’essai est proposé.
Ces tarifs sont très en deçà des 30 euros souvent cités, mais le prix de 15,60 € est une offre promotionnelle valable jusqu’au 31 décembre 2026 . Le tarif de référence est de 18,20 € HT par mois en paiement annuel.
Pour qui : les entreprises sous Microsoft 365, et les équipes RH, finance ou commerciales qui vivent dans Outlook et Teams.
## Aucun ne domine partout, c’est le contexte qui tranche
Les quatre assistants se sont rapprochés sur les tâches courantes. L’écart se creuse ailleurs : dans la longueur de document que l’outil encaisse, et dans les logiciels où il est déjà présent.
Sans contrainte d’écosystème, ChatGPT reste le point de départ le plus simple. Pour les documents longs et les analyses précises, la fenêtre d’un million de tokens de Claude fait la différence.
Si votre journée se passe dans Gmail et Docs, Gemini s’impose de lui-même. Si elle se passe dans Outlook et Teams, c’est Copilot.
Les quatre proposent une version gratuite ou un essai : le test coûte une demi-journée, l’abonnement coûte toute l’année.
Versions et tarifs relevés le 16 octobre 2026 sur les sites d’OpenAI, d’Anthropic, de Google et de Microsoft. Cette page est revue tous les trente jours.
Publicité
Article mis à jour le 16 octobre 2026 : GPT-6 est devenu le modèle par défaut de ChatGPT, Anthropic a renouvelé sa gamme Claude en version 5.5 et Google a lancé Gemini 4 Argon.
## Votre avis nous intéresse

entries.title: Prompt : VPC Subnet CIDR Planner
entries.content:
Modèle de prompt prêt à l'emploi : **VPC Subnet CIDR Planner**.
À copier dans le chat ou l'Atelier IA d'Ivass, en adaptant les parties entre ${…}.

---

---
name: vpc-subnet-cidr-planner
description: Plans and checks IPv4 subnet layouts for AWS, Azure, GCP or on-prem networks. Sizes each subnet from host counts plus growth and the provider's reserved addresses, allocates aligned CIDR blocks largest-first, and flags overlapping subnets, VPC ranges that clash with peered VPCs, VPNs or the docker0 bridge, public ranges, size limits, low headroom and single-zone layouts. Includes a stdlib Python planner with --self-test.
---

# VPC Subnet CIDR Planner

You help engineers carve a network into subnets that fit today, leave room to grow, and never collide with anything they will need to route to later. You turn "we need public, app and data subnets in two zones" into exact CIDR blocks, explain the numbers, and catch the overlaps that are painful to fix once workloads are running.

## Files in this skill

- `scripts/cidr_plan.py` - sizes and allocates subnets, lists usable host ranges and free blocks, and reports findings (Python 3 standard library only, uses `ipaddress`)
- `references/cidr-math-and-provider-rules.md` - prefix sizes table, alignment, reserved addresses and limits per provider, private ranges
- `references/subnet-layout-playbook.md` - tiered layouts, zone strategy, sizing Kubernetes pod subnets, avoiding overlaps with VPNs and peers, renumbering options
- `templates/subnet-plan.md` - a plan document for review or a pull request
- `examples/shop-platform-vpc.json` - an AWS /18 with legacy subnets, a peered analytics VPC and six new subnets in two zones

## Workflow

### 1. Gather the network facts
Ask for the provider, the VPC / VNet CIDR (or the range they may use), existing subnets, every network it must talk to (peered VPCs, VPNs, on-prem offices, partner links, other clouds), and the subnets they need: purpose, zone, hosts now, and expected growth. For Kubernetes, ask whether pods get VPC addresses (AWS VPC CNI, Azure CNI) because then pod count, not node count, sizes the subnet.

### 2. Run the planner
```
python3 scripts/cidr_plan.py examples/shop-platform-vpc.json
python3 scripts/cidr_plan.py plan.json --json
python3 scripts/cidr_plan.py --self-test
```
Exit code 1 means HIGH findings (overlaps, no space), 2 means bad input (host bits set, IPv6, overlapping VPC ranges).

### 3. Review the result
Fix HIGH findings first: an overlap with a peer or VPN cannot be routed and usually means picking a new VPC range now, while it is cheap. Use `references/subnet-layout-playbook.md` to adjust the layout (equal-sized subnets per zone, a spare block per tier, room for a third zone) and `references/cidr-math-and-provider-rules.md` to explain sizes. Re-run after each change.

### 4. Deliver
Fill `templates/subnet-plan.md` with the table, free blocks, findings and decisions. Offer Terraform or CLI snippets for the final blocks if asked.

## Example result
For `examples/shop-platform-vpc.json` (AWS [IP]/18): app subnets of 2,500 pods +60% growth get /20s (4,091 usable each) at [IP]/20 and [IP]/20; load balancer and data subnets get /25s (123 usable). Findings: HIGH legacy rds-b [IP]/25 overlaps rds-a [IP]/24; HIGH the peered analytics VPC [IP]/20 sits inside this VPC, so routing to it breaks; LOW only 20% of the space is left free.

## Rules

- Never propose a range that overlaps a known peer, VPN or on-prem network; ask for the full list if unsure.
- Plan for growth and a future zone; resizing a subnet in place is usually impossible.
- Keep IPv4 math exact; show usable counts after the provider's reserved addresses.
- Do not change live networks yourself; give a plan and the order of changes for the user to apply.
FILE:references/cidr-math-and-provider-rules.md
# CIDR Math and Provider Rules

## Prefix sizes (IPv4)
| Prefix | Addresses | AWS / Azure usable (-5) | GCP usable (-4) | Classic usable (-2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| /16 | 65,536 | 65,531 | 65,532 | 65,534 |
| /18 | 16,384 | 16,379 | 16,380 | 16,382 |
| /19 | 8,192 | 8,187 | 8,188 | 8,190 |
| /20 | 4,096 | 4,091 | 4,092 | 4,094 |
| /21 | 2,048 | 2,043 | 2,044 | 2,046 |
| /22 | 1,024 | 1,019 | 1,020 | 1,022 |
| /23 | 512 | 507 | 508 | 510 |
| /24 | 256 | 251 | 252 | 254 |
| /25 | 128 | 123 | 124 | 126 |
| /26 | 64 | 59 | 60 | 62 |
| /27 | 32 | 27 | 28 | 30 |
| /28 | 16 | 11 | 12 | 14 |
Each step of one in the prefix halves or doubles the block. Addresses = 2^(32 - prefix).

## Alignment
A block must start on a multiple of its own size: a /20 starts at x.x.0.0, x.x.16.0, x.x.32.0, ...; [IP]/20 is invalid (host bits set). Allocating largest blocks first keeps the space unfragmented; small subnets placed first can block every aligned slot for a big one.

## Reserved addresses per subnet
- **AWS:** first four (network, VPC router, DNS, reserved) and the last (broadcast) -> 5. VPC CIDR /16 to /28, subnets /16 to /28. Up to 5 CIDR blocks per VPC by default (secondary CIDRs can add space later).
- **Azure:** first four (network, gateway, 2 x DNS) and the last -> 5. Subnets up to /29. Some services need dedicated subnets (GatewaySubnet /27 or larger, AzureFirewallSubnet /26, AzureBastionSubnet /26).
- **GCP:** network, gateway, second-to-last and broadcast -> 4. Subnets are regional (not zonal), /29 smallest; secondary ranges for GKE pods and services.
- **Classic / on-prem:** network and broadcast -> 2 (/31 point-to-point links are a special case).

## Private and special ranges
- RFC 1918: [IP]/8, [IP]/12, [IP]/16.
- Carrier-grade NAT shared space [IP]/10 (RFC 6598): usable inside clouds, but check the ISP / VPN does not use it.
- Avoid: [IP]/16 (default docker0 bridge), [IP]/16 (link-local, cloud metadata), [IP]/24 and [IP]/24 (home routers, so VPN users clash), [IP]/16 (default VPC in many tools, so peers often clash).
- Public ranges inside a VPC make those internet addresses unreachable from it.

## Quick formulas
- Smallest prefix for N usable hosts with R reserved: 32 - ceil(log2(N + R)).
- Hosts with growth: ceil(hosts x (1 + growth)).
- Free space after a plan = VPC addresses - (existing + new + blocked peer ranges inside the VPC).
FILE:references/subnet-layout-playbook.md
# Subnet Layout Playbook

## Tiered layout per zone
| Tier | Holds | Typical size | Route |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public | load balancers, NAT gateways, bastion | /24 to /26 | internet gateway |
| Private app | VMs, containers, Kubernetes nodes and pods | largest, /20 to /22 | NAT gateway |
| Data | databases, caches, queues | /24 to /26 | no internet route |
| Spare | future tier or a third zone | keep one aligned block | - |
Use the same size per tier in every zone so a failover zone can carry the full load.

## Zone strategy
- At least two zones for anything production; three if the region and budget allow.
- Reserve the third zone's blocks now even if unused; it keeps the layout symmetrical.
- GCP subnets are regional, so plan per region instead of per zone.

## Sizing Kubernetes
- With AWS VPC CNI or Azure CNI every pod takes a VPC address: size app subnets by peak pods (nodes x max pods per node), plus surge during rolling updates (often +25%) and node replacement.
- Prefix delegation (AWS) or overlay networking (Calico, Cilium, kubenet, Azure CNI Overlay) moves pods to a separate range; then size by nodes and keep the pod CIDR clear of every peer.
- Keep the service CIDR (for example [IP]/16) clear of the VPC and peers too.

## Avoiding overlaps
- Collect every network you will ever route to: other VPCs and accounts, VPN clients, offices, partners, other clouds, and ranges used by acquired companies.
- Keep a central IP plan (spreadsheet or IPAM) and give each environment its own block, for example [IP]/16 prod, [IP]/16 staging, [IP]/16 dev.
- Do not pick [IP]/16, [IP]/16 or [IP]/24 to [IP]/24 for anything that VPN users reach.

## When something already overlaps
1. Prefer renumbering the smaller or newer side now (new VPC or a secondary CIDR, migrate, delete old).
2. If renumbering is impossible, use NAT (private NAT gateway, NAT on the VPN device) and route only translated ranges.
3. Overlapping subnets inside one VPC cannot be created on AWS / Azure / GCP; in documents they are usually typos, so verify the real values.

## Review checklist
- [ ] VPC range private and unique across all peers and VPNs
- [ ] every subnet aligned, inside the VPC and non-overlapping
- [ ] sizes include reserved addresses and growth
- [ ] same tier sizes in each zone; spare block kept
- [ ] at least 25% of the VPC left free
FILE:templates/subnet-plan.md
# Subnet Plan - <network name>

**Provider / region:** <aws eu-west-1>  **VPC CIDR:** <10.x.0.0/16>  **Owner:** <team>  **Date:** <date>
**Peers / VPNs checked:** <list of ranges>

## Subnets
| Subnet | Tier | Zone | Hosts now | Growth | CIDR | Usable | Route table |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | | | |

## Existing subnets kept
| Name | CIDR | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| | | |

## Free space
- Used or blocked: <n> of <total> (<x>% free)
- Spare blocks reserved for: <third zone / future tier>

## Findings and decisions
| Severity | Finding | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| | | |

## Rollout order
1. <create secondary CIDR / new VPC>
2. <create subnets and route tables>
3. <migrate workloads, remove old subnets>
FILE:examples/shop-platform-vpc.json
{
  "name": "shop platform, eu-west-1 production VPC",
  "provider": "aws",
  "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/18"],
  "existing": [
    {"name": "legacy bastion", "cidr": "[IP]/26"},
    {"name": "legacy rds-a", "cidr": "[IP]/24"},
    {"name": "legacy rds-b", "cidr": "[IP]/25"}
  ],
  "peers": [
    {"name": "office VPN (Istanbul)", "cidr": "[IP]/24"},
    {"name": "analytics VPC (peered)", "cidr": "[IP]/20"}
  ],
  "requests": [
    {"name": "public-a (load balancers)", "hosts": 40, "zone": "eu-west-1a", "growth": 0.5},
    {"name": "public-b (load balancers)", "hosts": 40, "zone": "eu-west-1b", "growth": 0.5},
    {"name": "app-a (EKS pods)", "hosts": 2500, "zone": "eu-west-1a", "growth": 0.6},
    {"name": "app-b (EKS pods)", "hosts": 2500, "zone": "eu-west-1b", "growth": 0.6},
    {"name": "data-a (databases, cache)", "hosts": 60, "zone": "eu-west-1a"},
    {"name": "data-b (databases, cache)", "hosts": 60, "zone": "eu-west-1b"}
  ]
}
FILE:scripts/cidr_plan.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""VPC subnet CIDR planner and checker (Python 3 standard library only).

Input: a network plan JSON file:
  {"name": "prod-eu", "provider": "aws", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/16"],
   "existing": [{"name": "legacy-db", "cidr": "[IP]/24"}],
   "peers": [{"name": "office vpn", "cidr": "[IP]/22"}],
   "requests": [{"name": "app-a", "hosts": 900, "zone": "eu-west-1a", "growth": 0.5}]}
  provider: aws | azure | gcp | generic. Reserved addresses per subnet: aws 5, azure 5,
  gcp 4, generic 2 (network + broadcast). Subnet size limits: aws /16../28,
  azure /8../29, gcp /8../29, generic /8../30.
  requests: hosts needed now; growth = extra fraction to reserve (default 0.3);
  optional "prefix" forces a size. Allocation is largest-first, aligned, lowest free address,
  never overlapping existing subnets or peer networks that sit inside the VPC.

Checks (severity):
  HIGH   OVERLAP_EXISTING   two existing subnets overlap
  HIGH   OUTSIDE_VPC        existing subnet not inside any VPC CIDR
  HIGH   PEER_OVERLAP       VPC CIDR overlaps a peered / VPN / on-prem network (routing breaks)
  HIGH   NO_SPACE           a request does not fit in the remaining space
  MEDIUM DOCKER_DEFAULT     VPC overlaps [IP]/16 (default docker0 bridge)
  MEDIUM PUBLIC_RANGE       VPC CIDR is not private (RFC 1918 / [IP]/10)
  MEDIUM PREFIX_LIMIT       requested or VPC prefix outside the provider limits
  LOW    LOW_HEADROOM       less than 25% of the VPC left free after the plan
  LOW    SINGLE_ZONE        all requests in one zone (no zone redundancy)
Usage:
  python3 cidr_plan.py plan.json
  python3 cidr_plan.py plan.json --json
  python3 cidr_plan.py --self-test
Exit code: 0 no HIGH findings, 1 HIGH findings, 2 bad input.
"""
import argparse
import ipaddress as ip
import json
import math
import sys

RESERVED = {"aws": 5, "azure": 5, "gcp": 4, "generic": 2}
HEAD_RESERVED = {"aws": 4, "azure": 4, "gcp": 2, "generic": 1}  # rest are at the end of the block
LIMITS = {"aws": (16, 28), "azure": (8, 29), "gcp": (8, 29), "generic": (8, 30)}
PRIVATE = [ip.ip_network(c) for c in ("[IP]/8", "[IP]/12", "[IP]/16", "[IP]/10")]
DOCKER = ip.ip_network("[IP]/16")


class PlanError(ValueError):
    pass


def net(cidr, what="cidr"):
    try:
        n = ip.ip_network(str(cidr).strip(), strict=True)
    except ValueError as e:
        raise PlanError(f"bad {what} {cidr!r}: {e}")
    if n.version != 4:
        raise PlanError(f"only IPv4 is supported: {cidr!r}")
    return n


def usable(prefix, provider):
    return max(0, 2 ** (32 - prefix) - RESERVED[provider])


def prefix_for(hosts, provider, growth):
    need = math.ceil(hosts * (1 + growth))
    lo, hi = LIMITS[provider]
    for p in range(hi, lo - 1, -1):
        if usable(p, provider) >= need:
            return p
    return None


def find_slot(vpcs, taken, prefix):
    for v in vpcs:
        if prefix < v.prefixlen:
            continue
        for cand in v.subnets(new_prefix=prefix):
            if not any(cand.overlaps(t) for t in taken):
                return cand
    return None


def plan(cfg):
    provider = str(cfg.get("provider", "generic")).lower()
    if provider not in RESERVED:
        raise PlanError(f"unknown provider {provider!r} (aws, azure, gcp, generic)")
    vpcs = [net(c, "vpc_cidr") for c in cfg.get("vpc_cidrs") or []]
    if not vpcs:
        raise PlanError("vpc_cidrs is empty")
    lo, hi = LIMITS[provider]
    findings = []

    def f(sev, code, where, msg):
        findings.append({"severity": sev, "code": code, "where": where, "message": msg})

    for v in vpcs:
        if not any(v.subnet_of(p) for p in PRIVATE):
            f("MEDIUM", "PUBLIC_RANGE", str(v), "not an RFC 1918 or [IP]/10 range; it may clash with real internet addresses")
        if v.overlaps(DOCKER):
            f("MEDIUM", "DOCKER_DEFAULT", str(v), "overlaps [IP]/16, the default docker0 bridge; containers on hosts in this VPC may lose routes")
        if provider == "aws" and not (16 <= v.prefixlen <= 28):
            f("MEDIUM", "PREFIX_LIMIT", str(v), "AWS VPC CIDR blocks must be /16 to /28")
    for i, a in enumerate(vpcs):
        for b in vpcs[i + 1:]:
            if a.overlaps(b):
                raise PlanError(f"vpc_cidrs overlap each other: {a} and {b}")

    existing = []
    for e in cfg.get("existing") or []:
        n = net(e.get("cidr"), "existing cidr")
        name = e.get("name") or str(n)
        if not any(n.subnet_of(v) for v in vpcs):
            f("HIGH", "OUTSIDE_VPC", name, f"{n} is not inside {', '.join(map(str, vpcs))}")
        for other_name, o in existing:
            if n.overlaps(o):
                f("HIGH", "OVERLAP_EXISTING", name, f"{n} overlaps {other_name} {o}")
        existing.append((name, n))

    taken = [n for _, n in existing]
    for p in cfg.get("peers") or []:
        n = net(p.get("cidr"), "peer cidr")
        name = p.get("name") or str(n)
        for v in vpcs:
            if v.overlaps(n):
                f("HIGH", "PEER_OVERLAP", name, f"{n} overlaps VPC {v}; traffic to the overlapping range cannot be routed both ways (renumber one side or use NAT)")
                taken.append(n)

    reqs = []
    for r in cfg.get("requests") or []:
        name = r.get("name") or "subnet"
        hosts = r.get("hosts", 0)
        if not isinstance(hosts, int) or isinstance(hosts, bool) or hosts < 1:
            raise PlanError(f"request {name!r}: hosts must be a positive integer")
        growth = r.get("growth", 0.3)
        if not isinstance(growth, (int, float)) or growth < 0:
            raise PlanError(f"request {name!r}: growth must be >= 0")
        if "prefix" in r:
            pfx = r["prefix"]
            if not isinstance(pfx, int) or not 8 <= pfx <= 30:
                raise PlanError(f"request {name!r}: prefix must be an integer 8..30")
            if not lo <= pfx <= hi:
                f("MEDIUM", "PREFIX_LIMIT", name, f"/{pfx} is outside {provider} subnet limits /{lo}../{hi}")
        else:
            pfx = prefix_for(hosts, provider, growth)
        reqs.append({"name": name, "hosts": hosts, "growth": growth, "zone": r.get("zone", ""), "prefix": pfx})

    allocs = []
    order = sorted(range(len(reqs)), key=lambda i: (reqs[i]["prefix"] if reqs[i]["prefix"] is not None else -1, i))
    for i in order:
        r = reqs[i]
        slot = find_slot(vpcs, taken, r["prefix"]) if r["prefix"] is not None else None
        if slot is None:
            f("HIGH", "NO_SPACE", r["name"], f"needs {r['hosts']} hosts (+{round(r['growth'] * 100)}% growth) and no free aligned block is left")
            allocs.append(dict(r, cidr=None, usable=0))
            continue
        taken.append(slot)
        u = usable(slot.prefixlen, provider)
        tail = RESERVED[provider] - HEAD_RESERVED[provider]
        allocs.append(dict(r, cidr=str(slot), usable=u,
                           first=str(slot[HEAD_RESERVED[provider]]) if u else "-",
                           last=str(slot[-1 - tail]) if u else "-"))
        if u < r["hosts"]:
            f("HIGH", "NO_SPACE", r["name"], f"/{slot.prefixlen} gives only {u} usable addresses for {r['hosts']} hosts")
    allocs.sort(key=lambda a: (a["cidr"] is None, ip.ip_network(a["cidr"]) if a["cidr"] else 0))

    total = sum(v.num_addresses for v in vpcs)
    used = 0
    inside = [t for t in taken if any(t.subnet_of(v) for v in vpcs)]
    for t in ip.collapse_addresses(inside):
        used += t.num_addresses
    free = total - used
    free_blocks = []
    for v in vpcs:
        rest = [v]
        for t in ip.collapse_addresses([x for x in inside if x.subnet_of(v)]):
            nxt = []
            for b in rest:
                if t.subnet_of(b):
                    nxt.extend(b.address_exclude(t))
                elif not b.subnet_of(t):
                    nxt.append(b)
            rest = nxt
        free_blocks.extend(sorted(rest))
    if total and free / total < 0.25:
        f("LOW", "LOW_HEADROOM", "plan", f"only {free / total:.0%} of the VPC address space is left free")
    zones = {r["zone"] for r in reqs if r["zone"]}
    if len(reqs) > 1 and len(zones) == 1:
        f("LOW", "SINGLE_ZONE", "plan", f"all requests are in {zones.pop()}; spread subnets over at least two zones")
    rank = {"HIGH": 0, "MEDIUM": 1, "LOW": 2}
    findings.sort(key=lambda x: rank[x["severity"]])
    return {"name": cfg.get("name", "network plan"), "provider": provider, "vpcs": [str(v) for v in vpcs],
            "existing": [{"name": n, "cidr": str(c)} for n, c in existing],
            "allocations": allocs, "total": total, "used": used, "free": free,
            "free_blocks": [str(b) for b in free_blocks], "findings": findings}


def report(res):
    out = [f"# Subnet plan: {res['name']}", "",
           f"Provider: {res['provider']} (reserves {RESERVED[res['provider']]} addresses per subnet)  VPC: {', '.join(res['vpcs'])}", "",
           "| Subnet | Zone | Hosts now | Growth | CIDR | Usable | First host | Last host |", "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
    for a in res["allocations"]:
        out.append(f"| {a['name']} | {a['zone'] or '-'} | {a['hosts']} | {round(a['growth'] * 100)}% | {a['cidr'] or 'NOT PLACED'} | "
                   f"{a['usable']} | {a.get('first', '-')} | {a.get('last', '-')} |")
    if res["existing"]:
        out += ["", "Existing subnets kept: " + ", ".join(f"{e['name']} {e['cidr']}" for e in res["existing"])]
    pct = res["free"] / res["total"] if res["total"] else 0
    out += ["", f"Address space: {res['used']} of {res['total']} used or blocked, {res['free']} free ({pct:.0%})",
            "Largest free blocks: " + (", ".join(sorted(res["free_blocks"], key=lambda c: ip.ip_network(c).prefixlen)[:6]) or "none"),
            "", "## Findings"]
    if not res["findings"]:
        out.append("- none")
    for x in res["findings"]:
        out.append(f"- **{x['severity']} {x['code']}** ({x['where']}): {x['message']}")
    return "\n".join(out) + "\n"


def self_test():
    cases = []

    def ok(name, cond):
        cases.append(bool(cond))
        print(("PASS " if cond else "FAIL ") + name)

    ok("aws /24 usable 251", usable(24, "aws") == 251)
    ok("generic /24 usable 254", usable(24, "generic") == 254)
    ok("gcp /29 usable 4", usable(29, "gcp") == 4)
    ok("900 hosts +50% on aws -> /21", prefix_for(900, "aws", 0.5) == 21)
    ok("250 hosts no growth aws -> /24", prefix_for(250, "aws", 0) == 24)
    ok("252 hosts no growth aws -> /23", prefix_for(252, "aws", 0) == 23)
    ok("too big for aws -> None", prefix_for(70000, "aws", 0) is None)
    base = {"provider": "aws", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/16"]}
    r = plan(dict(base, requests=[{"name": "a", "hosts": 200, "zone": "z1"}, {"name": "b", "hosts": 1000, "zone": "z2"}]))
    cid = {a["name"]: a["cidr"] for a in r["allocations"]}
    ok("largest first gets lowest block", cid == {"b": "[IP]/21", "a": "[IP]/23"})
    ok("clean plan has no findings", r["findings"] == [])
    aa = [a for a in r["allocations"] if a["name"] == "a"][0]
    ok("first/last host skip aws reserved", (aa["first"], aa["last"]) == ("[IP]", "[IP]"))
    g = plan({"provider": "gcp", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/16"], "requests": [{"name": "a", "hosts": 100, "growth": 0}]})["allocations"][0]
    ok("gcp reserves 2 head + 2 tail", (g["cidr"], g["first"], g["last"]) == ("[IP]/25", "[IP]", "[IP]"))
    r = plan(dict(base, existing=[{"name": "old", "cidr": "[IP]/22"}], requests=[{"name": "a", "hosts": 1000}]))
    ok("allocation avoids existing", r["allocations"][0]["cidr"] == "[IP]/21")
    r = plan(dict(base, existing=[{"name": "x", "cidr": "[IP]/24"}, {"name": "y", "cidr": "[IP]/25"}]))
    ok("overlap existing flagged", any(x["code"] == "OVERLAP_EXISTING" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan(dict(base, existing=[{"name": "x", "cidr": "[IP]/24"}]))
    ok("outside vpc flagged", any(x["code"] == "OUTSIDE_VPC" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan(dict(base, peers=[{"name": "vpn", "cidr": "[IP]/22"}], requests=[{"name": "a", "hosts": 900, "growth": 0}]))
    ok("peer overlap flagged", any(x["code"] == "PEER_OVERLAP" for x in r["findings"]))
    ok("allocation avoids peer range", r["allocations"][0]["cidr"] == "[IP]/22")
    r = plan({"provider": "aws", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/24"], "requests": [{"name": "a", "hosts": 200}]})
    ok("no space flagged", any(x["code"] == "NO_SPACE" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan({"provider": "generic", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/12"]})
    ok("docker default flagged", any(x["code"] == "DOCKER_DEFAULT" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan({"provider": "generic", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/16"]})
    ok("public range flagged", any(x["code"] == "PUBLIC_RANGE" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan({"provider": "aws", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/8"]})
    ok("aws vpc /8 flagged", any(x["code"] == "PREFIX_LIMIT" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan({"provider": "aws", "vpc_cidrs": ["[IP]/22"], "requests": [{"name": "a", "hosts": 400, "zone": "z1"}, {"name": "b", "hosts": 300, "zone": "z1"}]})
    ok("low headroom flagged", any(x["code"] == "LOW_HEADROOM" for x in r["findings"]))
    ok("single zone flagged", any(x["code"] == "SINGLE_ZONE" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan(dict(base, requests=[{"name": "a", "hosts": 10, "prefix": 30}]))
    ok("forced /30 on aws flagged", any(x["code"] == "PREFIX_LIMIT" for x in r["findings"]))
    r = plan(dict(base, requests=[{"name": "a", "hosts": 1000}]))
    ok("free blocks cover rest", sum(ip.ip_network(b).num_addresses for b in r["free_blocks"]) == 65536 - 2048)
    for bad, label in ((dict(base, vpc_cidrs=[]), "empty vpc"), (dict(base, vpc_cidrs=["[IP]/16"]), "host bits set"),
                       (dict(base, provider="oracle"), "unknown provider"), (dict(base, requests=[{"hosts": 0}]), "zero hosts"),
                       (dict(base, vpc_cidrs=["[IP]/16", "[IP]/17"]), "overlapping vpcs"),
                       (dict(base, vpc_cidrs=["fd00::/48"]), "ipv6")):
        try:
            plan(bad)
            ok(label + " rejected", False)
        except PlanError:
            ok(label + " rejected", True)
    print(f"{sum(cases)}/{len(cases)} passed")
    return 0 if all(cases) else 1


def main(argv=None):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Plan and check VPC subnet CIDR blocks.")
    ap.add_argument("file", nargs="?", help="network plan JSON")
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true", help="print machine-readable JSON")
    ap.add_argument("--self-test", action="store_true")
    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
    if a.self_test:
        return self_test()
    if not a.file:
        ap.error("give a plan JSON file or --self-test")
    try:
        cfg = json.load(open(a.file, encoding="utf-8"))
        res = plan(cfg)
    except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError, PlanError) as e:
        print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    print(json.dumps(res, indent=2) if a.json else report(res), end="" if not a.json else "\n")
    return 1 if any(x["severity"] == "HIGH" for x in res["findings"]) else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Méthode : Créer, entraîner et utiliser un modèle de machine learning
**Objectif :** Prédire des résultats à partir de données avec scikit-learn
**Source :** Python Full Course for Beginners — Programming with Mosh ([4:38:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_uQrJ0TkZlc&t=16680s))

1. Séparer les données en ensemble d'entrée (X) et de sortie (y)
2. Importer le classifieur : from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
3. Créer une instance du modèle : model = DecisionTreeClassifier()
4. Entraîner le modèle avec model.fit(X, y)
5. Effectuer des prédictions avec model.predict([['donnees']])

**Pièges signalés dans la vidéo :**
- Oublier de cocher l'option d'ajout de Python au PATH sous Windows empêche de suivre correctement les tutoriels.
- Laisser le projet configuré sur Python 2 (version legacy par défaut sur certains Mac) au lieu de Python 3.
- Mettre des guillemets autour d'une variable dans un print() affichera le nom de la variable sous forme de texte au lieu de sa valeur.
- Oublier que Python est sensible à la casse (écrire 'true' ou 'false' en minuscules provoque une erreur).
- La fonction input() renvoie TOUJOURS une chaîne de caractères (str), même si l'utilisateur tape un nombre. Tenter d'effectuer des calculs mathématiques directs dessus générera un TypeError.

entries.title: Correction powershell : L'outil pipwin n'est pas installé ou reconnu dans le PATH, provoquant une erreur de commande introuvable lors de son exécution.
entries.content:
## Erreur rencontrée (powershell, type : encoding)
```
> powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command [Console]::OutputEncoding=[Text.Encoding]::UTF8; $OutputEncoding=[Text.Encoding]::UTF8; $global:LASTEXITCODE=0; try { & ./main.ps1 } catch { Write-Error $_; exit 1 }; if (-not $?) { exit 1 }; exit $LASTEXITCODE
[Console]::OutputEncoding=[Text.Encoding]::UTF8; $OutputEncoding=[Text.Encoding]::UTF8; $global:LASTEXITCODE=0; try { 
& ./main.ps1 } catch { Write-Error $_; exit 1 }; if (-not $?) { exit 1 }; exit $LASTEXITCODE : Le terme «pipwin» n'est 
pas reconnu comme nom d'applet de commande, fonction, fichier de script ou programme exécutable. Vérifiez 
l'orthographe du nom, ou si un chemin d'accès existe, vérifiez que le chemin d'accès est correct et réessayez.
    + CategoryInfo          : NotSpecified: (:) [Write-Error], WriteErrorException
    + FullyQualifiedErrorId : Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.WriteErrorException
 

```

## Cause
L'outil pipwin n'est pas installé ou reconnu dans le PATH, provoquant une erreur de commande introuvable lors de son exécution.

## Code corrigé et vérifié (exécuté avec succès)
```powershell
$ivassPath = "C:\Users\[utilisateur]\Desktop\IvassAI"
if (-not (Test-Path $ivassPath)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $ivassPath -Force | Out-Null }
Set-Location $ivassPath

# Installation propre sans Pygame ni PyAudio (évite les erreurs de compilation MSVC)
pip install SpeechRecognition edge-tts pipwin --quiet
python -m pipwin install pyaudio

# Lancement direct
python ivass_assistant_live.py
```

## Code d’origine
```powershell
$ivassPath = "C:\Users\[utilisateur]\Desktop\IvassAI"
if (-not (Test-Path $ivassPath)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $ivassPath -Force | Out-Null }
Set-Location $ivassPath

# Installation propre sans Pygame ni PyAudio (évite les erreurs de compilation MSVC)
pip install SpeechRecognition edge-tts --quiet
pip install pipwin --quiet
pipwin install pyaudio

# Lancement direct
python ivass_assistant_live.py
```

entries.content:
# Méthode : Réaliser un projet de machine learning
**Objectif :** Créer, entraîner et évaluer un modèle prédictif à partir de données
**Source :** Python Full Course for Beginners — Programming with Mosh ([4:12:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_uQrJ0TkZlc&t=15176s))

1. Importer les données (souvent depuis un fichier CSV ou une base de données exportée).
2. Nettoyer les données (supprimer les doublons, les données non pertinentes ou incomplètes, et convertir les données textuelles en valeurs numériques).
3. Diviser le jeu de données en deux segments : un pour l'entraînement (ex: 80%) et un pour les tests (ex: 20%).
4. Créer un modèle en sélectionnant un algorithme adapté au problème (ex: arbres de décision, réseaux de neurones) via une bibliothèque comme Scikit-Learn.
5. Entraîner le modèle en lui fournissant les données d'entraînement pour qu'il détecte les motifs.
6. Faire des prédictions et évaluer leur précision.
7. Ajuster les paramètres du modèle ou changer d'algorithme pour optimiser les résultats si nécessaire.

**Pièges signalés dans la vidéo :**
- Oublier de cocher l'option d'ajout de Python au PATH sous Windows empêche de suivre correctement les tutoriels.

# exiftool

> Lit et écrit les métadonnées dans des fichiers.
> Plus d'informations : <https://exiftool.org/exiftool_pod.html>.

- Affiche les métadonnées EXIF d'un fichier donné :

`exiftool {{chemin/vers/fichier}}`

- Supprime toutes les métadonnées EXIF des fichiers donnés :

`exiftool -All= {{chemin/vers/fichier1 chemin/vers/fichier2 ...}}`

- Supprime les métadonnées EXIF GPS des fichiers image donnés :

`exiftool "-gps*=" {{chemin/vers/image1 chemin/vers/image2 ...}}`

- Supprime toutes les métadonnées EXIF des fichiers image donnés, puis ré-ajoute les métadonnées de couleur et d'orientation :

`exiftool -All= -tagsfromfile @ -colorspacetags -orientation {{chemin/vers/image1 chemin/vers/image2 ...}}`

- Avance d'une heure la date de prise de toutes les photos d'un répertoire :

`exiftool "-AllDates+=0:0:0 1:0:0" {{chemin/vers/répertoire}}`

- Recule d'un jour et deux heures la date de prise de toutes les photos JPEG du répertoire actuel :

`exiftool "-AllDates-=0:0:1 2:0:0" {{[-ext|-extension]}} jpg`

- Modifie uniquement le champ `DateTimeOriginal` en soustrayant 1,5 heure, sans conserver de sauvegardes :

`exiftool -DateTimeOriginal-=1.5 -overwrite_original`

- Renomme récursivement toutes les photos JPEG d'un répertoire à partir du champ `DateTimeOriginal` :

`exiftool '-filename<DateTimeOriginal' {{[-d|-dateFormat]}} %Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S%%lc.%%e {{chemin/vers/répertoire}} {{[-r|-recurse]}} {{[-ext|-extension]}} jpg`

## Modals and Popups

## Scroll

* [fullPage](https://github.com/alvarotrigo/fullPage.js) - A simple and easy to use plugin to create fullscreen scrolling websites (also known as single page websites).
* [ScrollMenu](https://github.com/s-yadav/ScrollMenu) - A new interface to replace old boring scrollbar.

## Table/Grid

## Frameworks

entries.title: Prompt : Strategic Business Blueprint Generator
entries.content:
Modèle de prompt prêt à l'emploi : **Strategic Business Blueprint Generator**.
À copier dans le chat ou l'Atelier IA d'Ivass, en adaptant les parties entre ${…}.

---

You are a senior strategy consultant (McKinsey-style, hypothesis-driven).

Your task is to convert a raw business idea into a decision-ready business blueprint.

Work top-down. Be structured, concise, and analytical. Avoid generic advice.

---

### 0. Initial Hypothesis
State 1–2 core hypotheses explaining why this business will succeed.

---

### 1. Problem & Customer
- Define the core problem (specific, not abstract)
- Identify primary customer segment (who feels it most)
- Current alternatives and their gaps

---

### 2. Value Proposition
- Core value delivered (quantified if possible)
- Why this solution is superior (cost, speed, experience, outcome)

---

### 3. Market Sizing (structured logic)
- TAM, SAM, SOM (state assumptions clearly)
- Growth drivers and constraints

---

### 4. Business Model
- Revenue streams (primary vs secondary)
- Pricing logic (value-based, cost-plus, etc.)
- Cost structure (fixed vs variable drivers)

---

### 5. Competitive Positioning
- Key competitors (direct + indirect)
- Differentiation axis (price, UX, tech, distribution, brand)
- Defensibility potential (moat)

---

### 6. Go-To-Market
- Target entry segment
- Acquisition channels (ranked by expected efficiency)
- Distribution logic

---

### 7. Operating Model
- Key activities
- Critical resources (people, tech, partners)

---

### 8. Risks & Assumptions
- Top 5 assumptions (explicit)
- Key failure points

---

### Output Format:

**Executive Summary (5 lines max)**  
**Core Hypotheses**  
**Structured Analysis (sections above)**  
**Critical Assumptions**  
**Top 3 Strategic Decisions Required**

entries.title: AnythingLLM vs Open WebUI vs LibreChat in 2026: Which Self-Hosted AI Interface Should You Use?
entries.content:
May 29, 2026
## AnythingLLM vs Open WebUI vs LibreChat in 2026: Which Self-Hosted AI Interface Should You Use?
By RunAIHome Team · 13 min read
local-ai open-webui anythingllm librechat self-hosted rag comparison
TL;DR : AnythingLLM is the fastest path to local document chat with zero terminal commands. Open WebUI is the most polished general-purpose local AI interface with the broadest feature set. LibreChat wins when your team needs multiple AI providers in a single UI with enterprise authentication. These three tools solve genuinely different problems — picking the wrong one means fighting your interface instead of using it.
AnythingLLM Open WebUI LibreChat
Best for Drag-and-drop document RAG, non-technical users Home lab power users, ChatGPT-like UX Teams needing multi-provider + LDAP/SSO
GitHub stars (May 2026) ~60K ~139K ~36K
Setup complexity Low — desktop app, zero-config Medium — Docker required Higher — Docker Compose + MongoDB + MeiliSearch
The catch RAG-first design feels clunky for pure chat Steeper initial setup than ATL desktop Heaviest stack; RAG is least mature of the three
Honest take : For most home-lab setups — one or two people, mostly chatting with LLMs plus occasional document Q&A — Open WebUI is the right call. It has more polish, the most active community (139K stars isn’t an accident), and extensibility through Python Pipelines when you outgrow the defaults. Use AnythingLLM only if document chat is your primary use case, and LibreChat only if you’re managing a team with real enterprise auth requirements.
## The Backend Question You Need to Answer First
All three tools are frontends , not inference engines. They connect to a model backend — Ollama , llama.cpp, LM Studio, or a cloud API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini). Before choosing a frontend, know which backend you’re running.
Ollama is the most common local backend in 2026, and all three frontends work seamlessly with it. If you’re mixing cloud APIs and need a single interface to juggle GPT-4o, Claude, and a local Llama model in the same conversation history, LibreChat is the only one of the three designed for that. For hardware sizing — how much VRAM you actually need to run the models behind these frontends — the VRAM guide for local LLMs covers that separately.
## The Three Contenders
## Open WebUI: The ChatGPT Replacement
Open WebUI has 139K GitHub stars — roughly 2.3× AnythingLLM’s count. That gap reflects real momentum: the project ships multiple releases per month, and the feature surface has grown fast. The core experience is a ChatGPT-like interface that works against Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible backend, with built-in RAG, TTS/STT, image generation hooks, a Python Pipelines plugin framework, and full multi-user management.
The deployment model is Docker-first. The standard single-command install:
docker run -d -p 3000:80 \
-v open-webui:/app/backend/data \
--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
You point it at a running Ollama instance (or cloud credentials) and you’re done. The admin panel creates user accounts, sets roles (admin or user), controls per-user model access, and shows token usage. Our Open WebUI multi-user setup guide covers the household/family server pattern in detail.
System requirements for Open WebUI itself are minimal — the container runs on 512MB RAM, 2 CPU cores. The ceiling comes from your model backend. Serving a 7B model to 5–10 concurrent users needs ~16GB system RAM and a GPU with 8GB+ VRAM. For a single-user setup on a mid-range card, an RTX 4060 Ti 16GB handles 7B–13B models with room left over.
Open WebUI’s strongest differentiator is the Pipelines framework — a plugin system where you write Python functions that intercept and modify the request/response stream. You can add rate limiting, custom logging, content filtering, or integrate external tools without modifying the Open WebUI codebase. Functions load through the admin UI; no container restart needed.
Recent 2026 additions worth noting: native Mistral TTS support (text-to-speech without an external provider — though if you want a cloned voice rather than a stock one, that’s a job for MOSS-TTS voice cloning ), Whisper STT preprocessing bypass for lower CPU/memory overhead, and a /ready endpoint for Kubernetes deployments. The project shows no signs of slowing down.
## AnythingLLM: The Document AI Platform
AnythingLLM came at local AI from the document-first direction, and that origin shapes everything about the product. The experience is built around workspaces — each one has its own document collection, LLM settings, and vector embeddings. Drag a PDF into a workspace, and the tool automatically chunks it, embeds it, and stores it in LanceDB (a built-in vector database). No vector DB setup, no chunking pipeline to configure, no embedding model to download separately.
The desktop app is AnythingLLM’s unique card. On Windows, macOS, or Linux, installation is a standard application installer — no Docker, no terminal, no API keys to manage for local Ollama usage. Open the app, and it can auto-detect and configure a local Ollama install. From zero to chatting with documents: under five minutes. For anyone not comfortable with Docker, this matters enormously.
Beyond the desktop app: Docker-based self-hosting is available (2GB RAM minimum for the app layer, 10GB disk), a managed cloud service ($25/month solo, $99/month business), a browser extension, and an Android mobile app released in 2026 that syncs across your self-hosted or cloud instance.
The no-code Agent Builder lets you create agents that chain document search, web browsing, SQL queries, and external API calls through a GUI — no code required. MCP (Model Context Protocol) support is built in, so you can expose AnythingLLM workspaces as MCP tools for Claude Desktop or other MCP-aware agents.
AnythingLLM supports 30+ LLM providers natively. An OS-level panel (activated with a keyboard shortcut) can appear over any application you have open and pull context from it directly into a chat — a genuinely useful feature for reading PDFs or browsing documentation.
Where it falls short: pure conversation without documents feels like using the wrong tool. The workspace model adds friction when you just want to ask a quick question. The chat interface is less polished than Open WebUI for continuous back-and-forth. If documents aren’t your primary use case, the UX fights you.
## LibreChat: The Multi-Provider Terminal
LibreChat’s core identity is universal provider access. A single conversation can switch between GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0, a local Llama 3.1 via Ollama, and a Mistral model — same conversation thread, same UI, same history format. That single-pane-of-glass approach for 15+ AI providers is LibreChat’s genuine differentiator over the other two.
The feature list is dense: conversation branching (fork at any message point), a code interpreter plugin, web search via Tavily or Google, artifacts (live HTML/React rendering inside the chat), model presets, per-user token usage tracking, and — the enterprise differentiator — comprehensive auth: local accounts, LDAP, Active Directory, Google/GitHub/Discord/OpenID social login. MCP support is also included.
That auth story is what makes LibreChat worth the heavier stack for teams. If you have 15 people and an existing LDAP directory, LibreChat integrates cleanly. Open WebUI’s user management is solid for households and small teams but doesn’t have LDAP. AnythingLLM has enterprise auth on its paid cloud tier, not in the free self-hosted version.
The deployment cost: Docker Compose running four services — LibreChat app, MongoDB (conversation and user storage), MeiliSearch (search), and an optional RAG API service. System requirements: 2GB RAM minimum, 4GB recommended for smooth multi-user operation. Node.js v20+ is required only if you skip Docker and install bare-metal. For a single-user home setup, that MongoDB + MeiliSearch overhead is hard to justify. For a team with real users, it’s the right foundation.
## Full Feature Comparison
Feature AnythingLLM Open WebUI LibreChat
Desktop app (no Docker) ✅ Mac, Win, Linux ❌ ❌
Mobile app ✅ Android ❌ (browser only) ❌
Built-in vector DB ✅ LanceDB ✅ built-in ✅ via RAG API service
RAG setup complexity Low (drag-and-drop) Medium Medium-high
Multi-provider single UI Limited Limited ✅ 15+ providers
Python plugin system ❌ ✅ Pipelines ❌
No-code agent builder ✅ ❌ ❌
MCP support ✅ native ❌ (via pipelines) ✅
LDAP / SSO auth Paid tiers only ❌ ✅ free
Conversation branching ❌ ❌ ✅
Code interpreter ✅ (via agent) ❌ ✅ plugin
TTS / STT built in ❌ ✅ (Mistral TTS, Whisper STT) ❌
Image generation ❌ ✅ AUTOMATIC1111, ComfyUI ❌
OS-level overlay panel ✅ ❌ ❌
Cloud-managed option ✅ $25–$99/mo Via third-party Via third-party
Open source (core) ✅ MIT ✅ MIT ✅ MIT
GitHub stars (May 2026) ~60K ~139K ~36K
## RAG: Where the Real Differences Lie
RAG support is where the three tools diverge most sharply, and it’s a common reason people pick the wrong one.
AnythingLLM was architected for RAG from day one. The workspace isolation model is the key feature: each workspace maintains separate vector embeddings, so a “company policy” workspace never surfaces results from a “personal journal” workspace during retrieval. Document support is broad: PDF, DOCX, TXT, Markdown, CSV, XLSX, PPTX, HTML, 50+ code file types, audio files. The built-in LanceDB handles chunking and embedding with sensible defaults — no tuning required to get useful results. For local private document AI , this architecture is genuinely well-suited.
Open WebUI has a capable built-in RAG pipeline that works well for the common cases: upload a document to a conversation, ask questions about it. Shared knowledge bases can be added across conversations. The chunking and embedding quality is solid. Where it falls short compared to AnythingLLM is organizing and managing large, structured document collections — the interface is chat-first and the document management layer is secondary.
LibreChat supports RAG through the optional RAG API Docker service. It’s functional but the least polished implementation of the three. If document Q&A is a primary workflow, LibreChat is not your best option.
## System Requirements Side-by-Side
These cover the frontend only — not the model backend:
AnythingLLM Desktop AnythingLLM Docker Open WebUI Docker LibreChat Docker Compose
RAM (app only) ~512MB 2GB 512MB 2GB min, 4GB rec
RAM (with 7B LLM) 8GB+ 8GB+ 8GB+ 8GB+
Disk space 2GB 10GB min 10GB 15GB+ (MongoDB + indexes)
Docker required ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅
Additional services none none none MongoDB + MeiliSearch
For GPU sizing behind these frontends, the best local AI models by VRAM tier guide maps which models fit which cards. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB vs used RTX 3090 comparison covers the sweet spot for a multi-user home AI server.
## Privacy: What Actually Leaves Your Machine
All three tools support a fully air-gapped setup — no data leaves your machine when you’re using a local inference backend like Ollama. None require accounts or call home for core functionality. For the broader picture of what telemetry local AI tools actually send, the local AI privacy audit covers that in detail.
One nuance with AnythingLLM: the cloud service ($25–$99/month) runs on isolated AWS instances managed by Mintplex Labs. That’s a different privacy posture than self-hosting. The desktop app and Docker versions are fully local. If you’re handling sensitive documents, use the desktop or Docker version — not the cloud subscription.
For teams using LibreChat or Open WebUI with cloud API providers (OpenAI, Anthropic), your prompts and documents do leave your machine on their way to those APIs. The local AI privacy audit breaks down which parts of the stack affect that boundary.
## Quick Picks by Setup Type
Solo home lab user, mostly chatting with LLMs: Open WebUI. Docker once, done. Best interface.
Non-technical user or family member who wants to ask questions about documents: AnythingLLM desktop app. Download and run, no Docker needed.
Home lab with 3–5 family members sharing a GPU server: Open WebUI with the admin multi-user config. Full walkthrough in the multi-user guide .
10-person team with existing LDAP and multiple cloud AI subscriptions: LibreChat. The multi-provider + LDAP story is unmatched.
Developer building local AI tools and AI coding integrations: Open WebUI (use Pipelines to connect to tools like Continue.dev or custom workflows). Its extensibility surface is the largest.
Someone who wants a no-code agent that can browse the web and search their documents: AnythingLLM’s Agent Builder.
## Frequently Asked Questions
Can I run AnythingLLM and Open WebUI on the same machine simultaneously?
Yes — they’re separate containers running on different ports and both connect to the same Ollama backend. Some setups run Open WebUI for general chat and AnythingLLM for document-specific workspaces. That said, it’s more to maintain than most personal setups need; pick one as your primary.
Does Open WebUI’s built-in RAG replace AnythingLLM for document chat?
For most users, yes. Upload a PDF, ask questions about it — Open WebUI handles that cleanly. AnythingLLM is worth the switch only if you have large structured document collections you query daily and need workspace-level retrieval isolation. The “company docs workspace” never leaking into the “personal notes workspace” is a real advantage at scale, but overkill for a handful of PDFs.
Is LibreChat free, or does it have paid tiers?
The LibreChat core is MIT-licensed and entirely free with no user limits or feature restrictions. There’s no official paid cloud version from the LibreChat team. Third-party managed hosting (Elestio, Railway, Spheron) charges $5–$30/month if you don’t want to self-host Docker.
What’s the difference between Open WebUI Pipelines and AnythingLLM agents?
Pipelines are Python functions that intercept the request/response stream — you write code to add logic (rate limiting, content filtering, custom tool calls). AnythingLLM agents are no-code GUI workflows that chain document search, web browsing, and API calls. Pipelines are more powerful and require Python; AnythingLLM agents are more accessible for non-coders but less flexible.
Which tool runs on the weakest hardware?
AnythingLLM Desktop app wins here — it runs on essentially any hardware for the frontend layer, and you can point it at a cloud API to skip local GPU requirements entirely. Open WebUI’s Docker container is lightweight too. LibreChat’s full Compose stack (MongoDB + MeiliSearch) is the most resource-hungry. On a machine with only 4GB RAM and no GPU, AnythingLLM Desktop + cloud API is the only comfortable option of the three.
